Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Ghana can grow the rice it eats Source : Prof. Maxwell Darko Asante 16 November 2026 8:37pm Prof. Maxwell Darko Asante ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
I have worked as a rice breeder in Ghana for the past two decades. During that time, people in Ghana and abroad have asked me a simple question.
“If you and your colleagues have released so many good rice varieties and developed technologies to help farmers grow them, why is Ghana still importing rice?”
My answer has always been clear. Research and development is a means to an end. For our work to make a difference at the national level, the private sector must invest and the government must put the right policies in place. Even the best rice variety will make little difference if farmers cannot get seed and fertiliser on time, lack the means to expand production, or harvest their crop and cannot find a buyer.
That is why I welcome the rice measures in the 2027 Budget. The government intends to use public procurement to create a market for Ghana-grown rice, link import licences to verified local purchases and end commercial rice imports by 2030. I believe Ghana can grow the rice it eats. The first thing I would do is buy the rice our farmers have already grown. [1]
Our rice farmers have taken a hard hit over the past two years. As recently as 13 November, farmers at Asutsuare reported that they were still holding unsold rice and that some stocks had spoiled. The Peasant Farmers Association of Ghana has reported similar difficulties across major rice-producing regions. Put yourself in the position of a farmer who has paid for seed, fertiliser, labour and harvesting and still has rice sitting in storage. What would persuade you to put money into another crop? [2, 3]
The government should release funds now to buy marketable Ghana-grown rice at farm gates, in warehouses and at mills. Where farmers have paddy, the government can work with millers to buy and process it. Milled rice that meets the required standards can go directly to schools, hospitals, prisons and other public institutions. Farmers and millers should be paid as soon as their deliveries are accepted. A farmer who is paid today can settle debts, buy inputs and prepare for the next season. That payment will do more to restore confidence than another announcement.
While the government buys the rice already in stock, public institutions should work out how much they will need for the next season. The government can then contract organised farmer groups, millers and rice entrepreneurs to supply agreed volumes. Before planting, farmers should know how much they are being asked to grow, what price they will receive, what grade they must meet and where to deliver. The Ghana-grown requirement should follow the public money, including when institutions buy through caterers or contractors.
The government should set aside the money when it awards the contracts and pay suppliers immediately upon acceptance of their deliveries. In the same Budget, the Finance Minister announced that GH¢29 billion was available for an early redemption offer on Domestic Debt Exchange Programme bonds due in February 2027. The Budget also made specific allocations for road works and maintenance. I would apply the same discipline to rice procurement. Farmers who wait months to be paid can miss the next planting season, even with a contract in hand. [1, 4]
The government already buys food for public institutions. Directing that spending towards Ghana-grown rice and paying promptly is the quickest step it can take to give farmers a reason to plant, millers a reason to invest and lenders a basis for financing the next crop.
The Minister for Food and Agriculture put annual demand at about 1.71 million metric tonnes of milled rice . He reported that Ghana produced about 960,000 tonnes of milled rice in 2025 , equivalent to roughly 56% of demand. That leaves a gap of about 750,000 tonnes of milled rice at the reported level of consumption. [5, 6]
To see what closing that gap would take, we have to start with the rice people eat and work backwards. Farmers harvest paddy. Some is set aside for seed, some is lost after harvest, and milling removes the husk and bran. Using the Feed Ghana Programme’s planning assumptions of 65% milling recovery, 13% post-harvest losses and 2.3% retained for seed, Ghana would need to harvest about 3.11 million tonnes of paddy to meet the reported demand. Better drying, storage and milling would give us more saleable rice from every tonne harvested. [7]
MoFA’s provisional 2024 baseline put the area under rice at 434,266 hectares , or about 1.07 million acres , and paddy production at 1.13 million tonnes . That works out to 2.6 tonnes per hectare . The baseline gives us a reference point for seeing how much land and seed different yields would require. [7]
At Dawhenya, some of the lead farmers we work with have harvested 8 metric tonnes of paddy per hectare , even in seed production fields, where we normally expect lower yields. That shows what our varieties can deliver under good management. A national average reflects the range of growing conditions across all rice farms. In 2023/24, USDA put average paddy yields at about 6.1 tonnes per hectare in Vietnam and 7.1 in China. [13] Given the area Ghana will need to bring into production and the conditions farmers will face across that area, I would plan on a national average of 4.5 to 5.0 tonnes of paddy per hectare .
Illustrative land and seed requirements at annual demand of 1.71 million tonnes of milled rice
Provisional scenarios pending MoFA’s latest acreage and yield figures. Estimates use Feed Ghana’s paddy-to-milled-rice assumptions. Seed quantities assume the full area is sown with certified seed at 80 kg per hectare. [7, 8]
At the provisional 2024 yield of 2.6 tonnes per hectare, Ghana would need to harvest nearly 1.2 million hectares a year . With a national average of 4.5 to 5.0 tonnes per hectare, meeting the same demand would take about 621,000 to 690,000 hectares harvested annually , or roughly 1.53 to 1.71 million acres. That is about half a million fewer hectares than would be needed at the 2024 yield.
Tanzania shows how expanding the area under rice can help a country reach self-sufficiency even at modest yields. In 2023/24, Tanzania’s Ministry of Agriculture reported that the area harvested rose by 22.4% and the average paddy yield increased from about 3.0 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare. The ministry put rice self-sufficiency at 112% that season. In Ghana, I would expand cultivation on suitable land while raising yields on existing rice farms. [14]
The 2027 Budget proposes bringing 100,000 additional hectares into production through rice development hubs, with yields of 5 to 6 tonnes per hectare in the hubs. We must also invest in farms outside the hubs. Where irrigation allows two crops a year, the same hectare can contribute two harvests. Both crops need seed, water and a buyer. At the national planning yield of 4.5 to 5.0 tonnes per hectare, each additional 100,000 tonnes of milled-rice demand would require roughly 36,000 to 40,000 more hectares harvested annually under the same assumptions. The 2030 plan should be sized for what Ghanaians are expected to consume by then. [1, 7]
Where will the seed come from for that area? Sowing the full area with certified seed at 80 kilograms per hectare , the lower end of MoFA’s recommended rate for broadcasting, would require about 49,700 to 55,200 tonnes annually . The final requirement will depend on the area actually planted, the share sown with certified seed and the mix of broadcasting, drilling and transplanting. [8]
Producing certified seed at that scale starts several seasons earlier with breeder and foundation seed. MoFA has already set targets for all three classes. The government should use the production plan to determine how much seed of each variety is needed, in which region and by what planting date. Research institutions should receive funding in time to produce breeder seed and support foundation seed multiplication. Seed companies with a record of producing quality seed should receive advance contracts to multiply and deliver seed, with enough time for inspection and certification. [7]
The same planning must cover fertiliser, access to machinery, irrigation and extension. Fertiliser must reach farmers when the crop needs it. Irrigation schemes must provide reliable water by planting time. Drying, storage and milling capacity must be ready when the extra paddy comes off the field. Each investment should have a delivery date tied to the season it is meant to serve.
Rice farmers need affordable access to machinery for land preparation, planting and harvesting. The 2027 Budget allocates GH¢800 million to procure machinery for Phase 2 of the government’s Farmer Service Centres. Farmers should be able to book tractors, seed drills and combine harvesters through the centres at published rates. A farmer who has seed and fertiliser ready still loses time if the tractor arrives after the planting window. [1]
We have seen what importers’ distribution networks can do for Ghana-grown rice. During the 2019–2020 push for local rice, Olam brought Ghana-grown jasmine rice to market under the Mama Gold brand, and Wilmar launched local rice under its Fortune and Viking brands. The new policy gives importers a reason to build on that experience. [9, 10, 11]
The test for an import licence should be straightforward. Can the importer show where the rice was grown, how much was bought, where it was delivered and who was paid? Each lot should count only once. Where the purchase is in paddy, a published conversion rate should be used to calculate its milled-rice equivalent. The government can then reduce quotas in step with verified supplies of Ghana-grown rice reaching consumers. Public institutions can start buying locally while those rules are being put in place.
The government must also stop rice from entering through unapproved routes. The General Agricultural Workers’ Union has raised concerns about rice smuggling. When traders evade duties and taxes, they can sell imported rice more cheaply and undercut Ghanaian producers and importers who pay what they owe. The National Rice Policy already calls for stronger customs valuation, border surveillance and anti-smuggling enforcement. Customs should step up checks at unapproved crossings and verify import permits and duty payments against shipment records while licensed imports continue. [11, 15]
At CSIR and in Ghanaian universities, we have developed improved aromatic rice varieties, most of them jasmine-type. At Dawhenya, we asked farmers and millers to assess improved varieties in the field and after milling. Farmers singled out CRI-Agyapa for its aroma, early maturity and good milling performance. The 2027 Budget records that MoFA secured 300 metric tonnes of Agyapa seed through the Korea Programme on International Agriculture for subsidised distribution to farmers. That is a practical example of how public investment can take a variety developed in Ghana from research plots to farmers’ fields. [1, 12]
Varieties are one part of the research we need. When we release a variety, farmers should also know how best to establish and manage it. That means testing when to plant, whether to broadcast, drill or transplant, and how to manage water, fertiliser, weeds, pests and diseases under local conditions. The work continues after the crop matures. We need practical ways to harvest and thresh on time, dry paddy to a safe moisture level, and store and mill it without avoidable losses or damage to grain quality. Research institutions should test these practices with farmers and millers and work with extension officers to get the results into use. [8]
It is expensive to produce rice in Ghana, and research can help bring those costs down. We should test planting methods that save seed or labour, fertiliser and water management that makes better use of inputs, and harvesting and milling practices that deliver more saleable rice from the same crop. In on-farm trials, I would measure what each practice does to the cost per tonne of paddy, and at the mill I would measure the cost per tonne of saleable rice. [11]
As production expands, new disease problems can emerge. When a popular variety is grown over large areas, changes in pathogen populations can erode the resistance farmers rely on. Changing rainfall and temperatures will also affect which varieties perform well and where. We need to monitor diseases in farmers’ fields and keep breeding and testing climate-smart varieties under Ghanaian conditions. Farmers must be able to grow them reliably, millers must be able to process them efficiently, and consumers must want to buy the rice again.
After two decades of breeding rice, I know how many seasons it takes to put a good variety in a farmer’s hands. When a variety begins to fail, the farmer needs a replacement for the next planting season. The rice policy should therefore provide sustained funding for this work from the outset. By the time farmers need a better-adapted variety, we should have tested it under Ghanaian conditions and be able to tell farmers how to grow it and millers how to preserve its quality.
With timely drying, proper storage and good milling, our jasmine-type varieties can match the aroma, taste and grain quality of the jasmine rice we import from Asia. If we bring costs down and deliver that quality consistently, Ghana-grown rice can compete on both price and quality.
Prof. Maxwell Darko Asante is Director of CSIR–Crops Research Institute, Chief Research Scientist in Rice Breeding, and an AfricaRice Council of Ministers laureate for excellence in rice research and development.
